name: functional-options
intent: Keep a constructor's required parameter list fixed while optional settings arrive as named configuration functions that are applied in order over built-in defaults, so the API can grow without breaking callers and without exposing a mutable configuration object.
problem: A constructor accumulates optional settings: every new setting changes the signature for all callers, zero values and booleans cannot be distinguished from 'not supplied', and a configuration struct has to be handed out (often by pointer, with nil meaning 'default') so callers can retain and mutate the very state the library depends on. The recurring decision is how to let an option set grow across the life of a public API while keeping meaningful defaults, source compatibility and a documented resolution rule for conflicting options.
context: Public constructors and factories of libraries, clients, servers and loggers whose option set grows across releases; languages without named or default arguments, or APIs that must stay source-compatible while options multiply; settings whose defaults are meaningful and whose combinations need a stated precedence (last wins) or explicit conflict handling.
benefits: The constructor signature never grows: new settings arrive as new option functions, so existing call sites keep compiling and nobody passes nil or a zero value to mean 'default'.
The default configuration is the simplest call - no arguments at all - with defaults chosen by the library rather than implied by the language's zero value.
Call sites are self-documenting: every option carries its name and value at the point of use, and options can be composed into reusable groups for common configurations.
Encapsulation: option functions operate on an unexported configuration value, so a caller cannot retain or mutate the library's internal state.

Options can carry behaviour, not just data: an option may allocate resources, wrap components (a TLS listener around a plain one), register callbacks or validate combinations that a flat parameter list cannot express.
Testability: production defaults stay untouched and a test overrides exactly the settings it exercises, so the test states its dependencies instead of reconstructing a full configuration.
tradeoffs: More surface than a parameter: each setting costs an exported option constructor (and, with interface-typed options, a type), so an option-heavy API accumulates boilerplate that one configuration struct writes in a single declaration.

Ordering and conflicts become part of the contract: the last option wins silently unless the library documents otherwise, and mutually exclusive options need explicit panic or error handling, so misconfiguration turns into a runtime rather than compile-time failure.

Options are opaque to reflection and serialization: unlike an options struct, a set of option functions cannot be enumerated, diffed, logged, merged or round-tripped from a configuration file, so declarative configuration needs a separate struct path.

Errors are awkward: an option that must report failure widens the option type (function returning an error) or defers validation to the constructor, and a partially applied target with invalid intermediate state exists while options run.
Discoverability depends on documentation: nothing in the type system lists the available settings, so users find options only through doc comments, naming conventions and generated documentation.

Allocation on the construction path: each option is a function value, usually a closure, and interface-typed options allocate an implementation per use - negligible for once-per-process construction, visible when a functional-options API is invoked per request or per message.

Required settings cannot be enforced by the compiler: a forgotten mandatory option surfaces at runtime (nil client, zero timeout) unless the constructor validates the assembled configuration and returns an error.

participants.responsibility: A first-class configuration function (or an interface with a single apply method) that knows how to change one setting of the target configuration; it carries its value in a closure and is applied to the target once per occurrence.

The exported factory (WithTimeout, WithoutRedirects, WithCredentials...) that closes over the caller's value and returns an Option; it documents the setting, its default and any conflict with sibling options.
Creates the target with documented non-zero defaults, applies every supplied option in the order given, then validates the assembled configuration and returns the target or an error.

The unexported configuration value (struct, record, builder or object under construction) that options mutate; it is never handed to callers, so no external reference can bypass defaults or mutate a built instance.
The documented baseline the constructor installs before applying options - the single source of truth for what happens when a caller passes nothing at all.

use_cases: Client and server constructors that must keep a stable signature while gaining credentials, timeouts, retries, interceptors and keep-alive settings across releases (gRPC-Go dialoptions, GCP Go SDK, Uber's internal service clients).
Loggers and instrumentation: severity, sampling, sinks and caller-annotation settings composed per component or per test.
Test fixtures: a production default plus a handful of overrides per scenario, without a builder class or a configuration file.
Reusable option groups baked into exported helpers for common deployments (insecure/local mode, tracing on, hardened defaults) that expand to several settings in one call.
Environment- or flag-driven construction where the option list is assembled at runtime from parsed input and applied to a single target.

OpenTelemetry SDK initialization: service name, endpoint, sampling ratio, resource attributes and exporter configuration composed via functional options with environment-variable fallback (otel-libs, OpenTelemetry Go resource construction).
SDK and library configuration for public APIs where the library must evolve without breaking caller code: adding a new tracing exporter or timeout setting does not change existing call sites.
Kubernetes operator and controller configuration where resources need environment-driven defaults but also explicit per-deployment overrides (o11y.Init, otelhelper.Setup patterns).
Database and message-broker client pools: connection limits, timeouts, TLS and credentials wired at construction time; per-query options (context, routing keys) stay out of the constructor.
HTTP middleware chain composition where each middleware is an option that wraps the next handler, enabling selective instrumentation without a fixed middleware list.
Feature-flag-driven service construction where the enabled feature set determines which options are applied, allowing a single NewService constructor to produce different service variants.
gRPC and Protobuf code generation integration where generated builder types expose functional options for fields that were not known at the time the proto was compiled.

gRPC-Go connection setup uses typed DialOption values such as WithUnaryInterceptor, WithChainStreamInterceptor and WithDefaultCallOptions to grow Dial/NewClient configuration without changing the constructor signature (grpc-go).

OpenTelemetry Go's TracerProvider is assembled with options such as sdktrace.WithBatcher, WithResource and WithSampler, composing exporter, resource and sampling choices at initialization (OpenTelemetry Go).

Kubernetes controller-runtime exposes typed per-operation options such as MatchingLabels, FieldOwner, DryRun and FieldValidation for client CRUD calls, keeping method signatures stable while extending request behavior (controller-runtime).
avoid_when: The option set is data: when configuration comes from files, environment variables or a control plane and must be validated, diffed or reloaded, a plain options struct is simpler and serializable.
The language already has named and default arguments (Kotlin, Swift, C#, Python, Ruby, Scala): the signature itself carries the optional named settings, and option functions only add indirection.
One or two optional flags that never grow: a plain parameter, a boolean or a small overload is clearer.
Required settings dominate: options cannot enforce presence, so everything mandatory belongs in positional parameters and options cover only the optional remainder.
Construction happens per request in a hot path and the option set is fixed: a pre-built configuration value copied in avoids closure allocation and repeated validation on every call.
anti_patterns: Options that overwrite each other silently: a single-use setting (interceptor, hook, listener) installed twice keeps the last value instead of failing, so callers cannot tell which configuration won.
Option functions with effects beyond the target — starting background work, opening files, mutating shared defaults — so applying an option twice or in a different order changes program behaviour.

Stringly-typed option maps ( kwargs, map[string]any, an options hash) used instead of typed options: misspelled settings are ignored, the documented defaults never apply and no tool can complete the option names.

Two overlapping configuration paths on one constructor (an options struct and option functions for the same settings) with different precedence rules, so the effective configuration depends on which path the caller happened to use.
Sharing one option value or one mutable configuration target across instances, so configuration applied to one object leaks into another.

Mixing per-request data into construction-time options: embedding request-scoped values (tokens, trace IDs) in options that are applied once at startup causes data to persist across requests when the option is reused.
Options that return an error but are applied via a void option type, silently dropping the error or panicking instead of surfacing it through a wider return type or final validation step.
A configuration struct passed by pointer and handed back to callers, allowing external code to mutate defaults after construction and before the constructed object uses it.
design_principles: Open/closed principle: the constructor signature stays closed to modification while new option functions extend the configurable surface.
Encapsulation: callers configure the object without ever seeing or retaining the configuration value, which only the constructor owns.
Single responsibility: one option sets exactly one setting; the constructor alone assembles, validates and publishes.
Least surprise: documented non-zero defaults plus an explicit 'later option wins' rule make the effective configuration predictable and testable.
Fail fast: invalid or conflicting combinations are rejected by the constructor or a terminating validation step before a live object exists.
best_practices: Keep the option target unexported and the option type exported; apply every option in the order supplied inside the constructor.

Name options With<Setting> (Without<Setting> when the default is on), document the default in the option's own doc comment and attach an example to the option function so documentation lives next to the setting.
State precedence and conflict behaviour in the package documentation, and make single-use options loud: panic or return an error when one is installed twice.
Give options that can fail a way to report it (an option type that returns an error, or a validation step the constructor calls) instead of panicking on caller input.
Start from documented non-zero defaults, never from the language's zero value, and never require a nil or zero sentinel to select the default.
Provide reusable option groups — and an equivalent options struct wherever configuration must be data — so declarative and programmatic callers share one set of defaults and one validation rule.
Prefer concrete option types (structs with an Apply method) over interface{} when testability and mocking are priorities; interface-based options allow co-located apply logic and easier substitution.
Use namespaced option groups (e.g., wireup.Options.WithCredentials, .WithTimeout) to improve discoverability and avoid polluting the top-level namespace for APIs with many options.
Separate construction-time wiring from per-request data: use options for dependencies and infrastructure (clients, loggers, TLSConfig) and context for request-scoped values (tokens, trace context).
Document the 'last option wins' rule explicitly and check for incompatible combinations (e.g., TLS and Insecure) before returning from the constructor, failing fast with a clear error.
For hot-path construction (per-request, per-message), pre-build a default configuration and copy it, avoiding repeated closure allocation and validation on every call.
When adding new options, introduce them as non-breaking additive changes; avoid making previously mandatory parameters optional or changing defaults of existing options in released APIs.
Consider interface-based options when options share validation logic or when the same option type applies to multiple target types, reducing code duplication across option implementations.
Use functional options in a 'wireup' or 'config' package layer that composes clients for testability: tests can pass mock implementations via options without reaching into internal state.
sources: Dave Cheney, Functional options for friendly APIs (dotGo 2014 talk text, 17 October 2014) — variadic option functions over defaults, error-returning options, groups of options, and the comparison with configuration structs.

Rob Pike, Self-referential functions and the design of options (command center blog, 24 January 2014) — the originating idea: an option is a function that sets a value on the target and can return its inverse.
Bytesize Go, 10 years of functional options and key lessons learned along the way (2024) — a decade of real-world usage, practical dos and don'ts, and evolution of the pattern in production systems.
FollowTheProcess, 3 Levels of Functional Options (2024) — progressive sophistication levels for the pattern, from basic to advanced usage patterns.
Functional Options vs Builder vs Config Struct in Go: Pick One — DEV Community (2025) — detailed comparison of configuration patterns, when each applies, and trade-offs between them.
Beyond functional options in Go — Felesatra.moe (2023) — critical analysis of the pattern's limitations, including order-sensitivity problems and when options structs are preferable.

Silent Gopher, Functional Options in Go: The Pattern Behind Clean Service Constructors (2025) — separating constructor-level configuration from per-request data; option functions for wiring, context for request-scoped values.
Smarty, Functional options pattern in Go: Flexibility that won't make future-you sigh loudly (2025) — namespaced options, SDK design, and backward-compatible API evolution.
Pete Davison, Better Functional Options (2024) — interface-based options for improved testability and co-location of apply logic.
Dennis O'Keeffe, Interface-based functional optionals in Golang (2025) — interface variant for flexibility and extensibility.
Uber Go Guide, Style Guide — discussion of functional options implementation approaches and when to avoid closures.
OpenTelemetry Go SDK, resource.New() functional options migration — PR #1235 demonstrates the pattern's adoption in standard infrastructure libraries.
gRPC-Go DialOptions, github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/master/dialoptions.go — production-scale usage of functional options in a widely-deployed RPC framework.
golang.design/research/generic-option/ — research on generic-based functional options in Go.
